title: Jambavan wakes Hanuman
hookLine: the strongest one on the beach hasn't said a word, so an old bear sits down and tells him his own story; why Hindus still sing it back to him
carry: strength remembered: why Hindus sing the Chalisa
last: NO ONE CAN PROMISE A HUNDRED.

lines: NOT ONE WORD IN THE COUNT.
cards: Some people never put their hand up. Not because they can't do the thing, but because it hasn't occurred to them that they could. On the beach, while the others called out their numbers, Hanuman sat to one side, silent.
Valmiki doesn't give him a line in the whole count. So Jambavan, the oldest one there, the one who knows everybody's story, gets up, walks over, and sits down beside him.

teach.b: Jambavan tells Hanuman his own story. Your mother was Anjana. Your father is Vayu, the wind.
As a baby you saw the sun coming up, thought it was a ripe fruit, and jumped for it, straight into the sky.

teach.h: THE SUN, THE THUNDERBOLT, THE JAW.
teach.b: Indra, king of the gods, threw his thunderbolt, you fell, and your jaw was struck. In Sanskrit the jaw is hanu, and that's where your name comes from. Then Jambavan says what he came to say: you have your father's speed.
Hanuman stands up. Valmiki describes him growing, filling with strength, roaring until the others cheer.
He climbs Mount Mahendra to push off from, and there the Kishkindha Kanda, the book of the monkey kingdom, ends: on a mountaintop, before the jump. Why did he need reminding?

teach.h: THE CHALISA SINGS HIS STORY BACK.
teach.b: Valmiki doesn't fully say; a story in the last book, which many scholars think was added later, says sages made him forget his strength until someone recalled it. Here's what Hindus do with this scene.
Jambavan woke Hanuman's strength by telling him his story, and families do the same in prayer.
The Hanuman Chalisa, forty verses sung in Hindu homes everywhere, often on Tuesdays and Saturdays, retells his deeds, the baby who took the sun for a sweet fruit among them.
People sing it before exams, surgeries, long drives, whenever they're afraid.
And many teachers read the beach as the soul's own story: the atman, the true self, is never weak, only forgetful, and a guru's work, like Jambavan's, is to remind it.

how: Jambavan reminding Hanuman of his strength is one of the best-loved scenes in Hindu storytelling, and many families sing the Hanuman Chalisa, which retells Hanuman's deeds, on Tuesdays and Saturdays or before something they're afraid of.

games.q: your little cousin asks why Nani sings the Hanuman Chalisa the night before something scary. by today's story, what fits?
o: it tells Hanuman's story back, the way Jambavan did, so his strength is remembered.
it's a lucky charm; the words don't matter.
it's only for people who are already brave.
games.why: Jambavan woke Hanuman's strength by telling him his own story. the Chalisa retells his deeds, so families call that strength to mind when they're afraid.

practice: Sit tall, feet on the floor. On each breath out, say silently: Jai Hanuman, victory to Hanuman, the way many families do before something hard.

If you'd rather not pray, recall one time your own strength showed up, and tell it to yourself the way Jambavan would: where you were, what you did, how it turned out. Let each breath in come a little fuller.

wordCard.voice: Hanu, the Sanskrit word for jaw, struck by Indra's thunderbolt when Hanuman was a baby, and the source of his name.

orig.note: Sanskrit hanumān, often explained as 'having a (notable) jaw', from hanu, jaw.

carryVoice: Your line: strength remembered: why Hindus sing the Chalisa. A new book of the epic starts tomorrow. Until then.
